doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: Deadlines and Brookmeyer's advice on writing
summary: Deadlines help him; he wrote overnight for Callaway and the New York Philharmonic, and Brookmeyer threw away two days of writing.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. It’s nice that you have that liberty now to make those kind of choices. Sliding back to composing and arranging, I caught this quote, probably from your website, that you said, “Deadlines are great inspiration.”

Well I used to put off everything ‘til the last minute, including getting to the airport at the last minute. And as I became older I got tired of all the pressure I was putting myself under. So I get to the airport two hours in advance always. And if I have a chart – well I’ll give you an example. I’m working on a Valentine’s Day concert. That’s two and a half months away. The music is almost all arranged for that. And I don't know, I don’t want to be in a panic situation but deadlines – I once had to write something overnight for Ann Hampton Callaway and the New York Philharmonic, an arrangement on “I Hear

Music” [scats]. So I was up all night doing that. I had to do it. I said yes to the gig. So deadlines are great to get you off your can to get it done. And you know Bob Brookmeyer used to say, when he had a writing assignment, he’d start in advance and he would write and throw away everything that he wrote in the first two days, to get rid of the B.S. and get the juices flowing and to get honest with himself. That’s tough, to throw away stuff. But that was a lesson well learned.
